bce 2782-07-20.label: BCE 2782-07-20 — First Apokatastasis
bce 2782-07-20.description: First *apokatastasis*: I-Akhet-1 coincides with heliacal rise of Sopedet (Sirius). This defines the datum of the caniucular calendar: *horus* year 0, hrw 0-I-Akhet-1.

bce 1322-07-20.label: BCE 1322-07-20 — Second Apokatastasis
bce 1322-07-20.description: Second *apokatastasis*: I-Akhet-1 again coincides with heliacal rise of Sopedet (Sirius), in the middle of the New Kingdom.

139-07-20.label: CE 139-07-20 — Third Apokatastasis
139-07-20.description: Third *apokatastasis*: I-Akhet-1 coincides with heliacal rise of Sopedet. Identified by Censorinus (Lull, p.95).

bce 559-10-19.label: BCE 559-10-19 — Papyrus Louvre 7848
bce 559-10-19.description: Date from Papyrus Louvre 7848 with both civil and lunar dates recorded (Lull, p.94, date there III-Shemu-13).

bce 238-03-07.label: BCE 238-03-07 — Canopus Decree
bce 238-03-07.description: Date of the Canopus decree, which attempted to add an intercalary day every 4 years to align the civil and astronomical years (Lull, p.76, date there I-Peret-17).

bce 237-08-23.label: BCE 237-08-23 — Edfu Temple Inscription (25-yr lunar cycle)
bce 237-08-23.description: Inscription in the Ptolemaic Edfu temple showing Egyptians knew the 25-year lunar cycle (Lull, p.92, date there III-Shemu-7).

bce 212-08-17.label: BCE 212-08-17 — Edfu Temple Inscription II
bce 212-08-17.description: Second inscription in Edfu temple confirming knowledge of the 25-year lunar cycle (Lull, p.92, date there III-Shemu-7).

384-07-23.label: CE 384-07-23 — Theon's Heliacal Rise
384-07-23.description: Heliacal rise of Sopedet (Sirius) according to computation by Theon of Alexandria (Lull, p.98, date there I-Akhet-1).

bce 688-06-11.label: BCE 688-06-11 — Papyrus Louvre E3228d
bce 688-06-11.description: Earliest document with a perfect Egyptian chronology: hieratic Papyrus Louvre E3228d, year 3 of king Taharqa (Lull, p.105, date there I-Peret-10).

bce 46-01-01.label: BCE 46-01-01 — Julian Calendar Reform
bce 46-01-01.description: Julius Caesar, advised by the Egyptian astronomer Sosigenes, introduces the Julian calendar with a 365.25-day year, directly derived from Egyptian solar calendar knowledge.
